items.title: Keshav Enterprises
items.subtitle: Intern · India
items.summary: Built the data and ML backbone for an SME manufacturer: an ELT pipeline replacing spreadsheet tracking, a RAG system for grounded customer replies, and an evaluation harness that decided which forecasting models were allowed to ship.
bullets: Architected an end-to-end ELT pipeline in Python and PostgreSQL, normalizing sales inquiry and order data across 4 relational entities to replace manual spreadsheet tracking for an SME manufacturer

Built a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using ChromaDB vector search and the Claude API to auto-draft grounded customer replies, constraining outputs to retrieved catalog data to eliminate hallucinated pricing

Designed and ran an ML evaluation harness benchmarking Prophet time-series forecasts against a naive seasonal baseline across 8 product lines, using MLflow to gate model deployment — correctly rejected the more complex model in 6/8 cases due to limited (24-month) history

Achieved a 74% relative MAPE reduction (29.4% → 7.6%) with Prophet on the tractor counterweight line, the product with a sustained growth trend, validating that the harness caught a genuine case for deployment
commentary: The most useful result here was a negative one. The evaluation harness rejected the fancier Prophet model on 6 of 8 product lines, because 24 months of history usually isn’t enough to beat a seasonal baseline.
The RAG replies are constrained to retrieved catalog data on purpose: a made-up price in a customer email is worse than no draft at all.

items.title: Change Assurance Runtime
items.subtitle: for AI Coding Agents · VT Hacks 14
items.summary: A local-first Windows runtime that puts AI coding agents under independent supervision: every process they spawn is attributed, every action is journaled in a tamper-evident log, and every change ships with a signed passport.
bullets: Built a local-first Windows runtime using kill-on-close Job Objects and restricted-token process launches to attribute every descendant process by PID, image path, and command line

Designed a tamper-evident, hash-chained event journal with end-to-end replay verification and a signed Ed25519 Change Passport capturing intent, authority, evidence, and outcomes for every agent action
Shipped three clients (Textual TUI, CLI, Electron/React desktop) against one frozen OpenAPI contract of 66 operations, 61 routes, and 110 typed schemas
Validated by a threat-model review (15 of 16 findings fixed) and 1,022 passing tests
commentary: The question behind this one: when an AI agent changes your machine, how do you prove what it actually did? Job Objects answer “which process,” the hash chain answers “in what order,” and the signed passport answers “on whose authority.”
Freezing the OpenAPI contract early is what let three different clients be built against it in parallel during a hackathon.

bullets: Discovers postings from public Greenhouse and Lever job-board APIs and other public boards on a GitHub Actions schedule, so there is no server to maintain

Backed by a test suite covering discovery quality, queueing, pipeline limits, and workflows
commentary: Built to solve my own problem. Everything runs on free infrastructure, so it costs nothing to leave running every morning.

items.title: Regime Detection
items.subtitle: & Adaptive Trading Strategies
items.summary: A Gaussian Hidden Markov Model that detects market regimes from SPY and VIX data, plugged into a cost-aware backtester.
bullets: Built a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) in Python to detect market regimes from SPY/VIX data using volatility, momentum, liquidity, and volume features

Developed a transaction-cost-aware backtesting framework with filtered probability inference, benchmarked against K-Means and momentum strategies; trained on 2015–2020 and tested out of sample on Jan 2021 – May 2026 (5 bps costs)
Achieved a 57.97% return (Sharpe 0.83) with ~34% lower volatility and a −15.3% max drawdown vs. −24.5% for Buy-and-Hold
commentary: An HMM gives probabilities, not labels. Using filtered probabilities in the backtest keeps it honest, since each decision only sees data available at that moment.
Benchmarking against K-Means and plain momentum is what makes the result mean something beyond “it made money in a backtest.”

items.title: Fork-Join Thread Pool
items.subtitle: Work-stealing task parallelism in C · CS 3214
items.summary: A fork/join framework for parallel divide-and-conquer algorithms, built up in stages from a single-lock work-sharing pool to a work-stealing pool with per-worker deques. Built with a partner.
bullets: Implemented a thread pool and futures API (submit, future_get, shutdown) in C with pthreads, evolving it from a single-lock work-sharing queue to per-worker deques with work stealing
Prevented deadlock with helping: a worker that joins a not-yet-started task executes it inline, while external threads wait instead of helping
Replaced the global lock with finer-grained per-worker locking, keeping each task's state change atomic with its removal from a queue so exactly one thread runs it
Kept idle workers blocked on condition variables (no busy-waiting), checked for data races with Helgrind, and benchmarked parallel speedup on 32-core Xeon machines
commentary: The subtle part is the join. A worker that waits on a future nobody has started yet can deadlock the pool, so instead it “helps” and runs that task inline.
Moving from one global lock to per-worker deques is where the speedup shows up, and also where Helgrind earns its keep.

items.title: Minibash
items.subtitle: A bash-subset shell in C · CS 3214
items.summary: A command-language interpreter implementing a subset of bash: pipelines, redirection, variables, command substitution, and control flow, with every job running in its own process group. Built with a partner.
bullets: Built a shell in C that parses scripts with the Tree-sitter bash grammar and runs simple commands, pipelines, && / || lists, if/elif/else, and for/while loops with break
Launched processes with posix_spawnp instead of fork + exec, wiring pipes and file redirection (including |& and >&) through spawn file actions and giving each job its own process group
Implemented quoting, variable expansion ($?, $$, ${var}), and $(…) command substitution, matching bash's exit-status rules (last pipeline stage; 128 + signal number)
Tracked child processes via SIGCHLD and waitpid, and verified memory safety under Valgrind
commentary: Using posix_spawnp instead of fork + exec means every pipe and redirection has to be declared up front as a spawn file action, a stricter way to think about what a child process inherits.
Exit statuses are the details you only notice when a script behaves differently from real bash: the last pipeline stage wins, and a process killed by a signal reports 128 + the signal number.

items.title: Malloc Lab
items.subtitle: A 64-bit dynamic memory allocator in C · CS 3214
items.summary: My own malloc, free, and realloc: a 64-bit allocator tuned to balance space utilization against throughput on trace-driven benchmarks. Built with a partner.
bullets: Implemented mm_malloc, mm_free, and mm_realloc returning 16-byte-aligned blocks, going beyond the implicit-free-list baseline the assignment disallowed as a final design
Designed the heap block layout and free-block organization, with splitting and coalescing to limit fragmentation
Tuned against a performance index weighting space utilization (60%) and throughput (40%) using the course's trace-driven driver
Encapsulated pointer arithmetic in static helper functions and guarded invariants with assertions to keep untyped memory code debuggable
commentary: Allocator design is a trade-off you can put a number on: the grading index weights space utilization 60% and throughput 40%, so every layout decision shows up in the score.
When one wrong offset can silently corrupt the heap, small static helpers and assertions are what keep the code debuggable.

items.title: The Streaming Effect
items.subtitle: How streaming reshaped the music industry · Data science team project
items.summary: A four-person data science study of how streaming changed the music industry from 2000 to 2025: song length, revenue by format, and genre popularity, built on data we scraped and cleaned ourselves.
bullets: Scraped Billboard Hot 100 year-end charts for 2000–2025, using Playwright for Billboard's dynamically loaded pages and pandas.read_html on Wikipedia tables for 2000–2005, then filled missing ranks and removed duplicates across sources
Built the song-genre dataset: when the Spotify and YouTube APIs proved too rate-limited and sparse, scraped MusicBrainz and normalized its many subgenres to main genres verified against Wikipedia
Found that the decline in average Hot 100 song length roughly doubled in rate after Billboard began counting streams in 2014, since each stream earns chart points regardless of length

Showed with RIAA revenue data that streaming overtook other formats around 2015–2016, averaging $8.2B per year in the streaming era versus $0.2B before it, visualized with line, stacked bar, pie, and heatmap charts
commentary: The plan changed mid-project: the Spotify and YouTube APIs were too rate-limited and sparse for genre data, so we switched to scraping MusicBrainz and mapping its subgenres to main genres.

items.title: The Blooper Reel
items.subtitle: Dead ends, plot twists, and negative results
items.summary: You found the secret profile. Every highlight on this site has a take that didn’t make the trailer: the model that lost, the API that gave up, the lock that deadlocked. These are the ones I learned the most from.
bullets: The fancier forecasting model lost: Prophet failed to beat a naive seasonal baseline on 6 of 8 product lines, so the harness shipped the simpler one
Plan A died mid-project: the Spotify and YouTube APIs were too rate-limited for genre data, so the team switched to scraping MusicBrainz
A thread pool can deadlock itself when a worker waits on a task nobody has started; the fix was to have it run that task inline
One wrong pointer offset silently corrupts a heap, which is why the allocator lives behind small helpers and assertions
